content: Breast pain, also known as mastalgia, is a frequently encountered symptom in general surgical practice. Breast discharge, on the other hand, is typically considered abnormal unless it occurs in the context of pregnancy or lactation. Differential Diagnosis for Breast Discharge: Breast discharge can result from a variety of conditions, including: Breast abscess, which is a localized collection of pus within the breast tissue. Breast cancer, which may present with nipple discharge, particularly if it is bloody or unilateral. Chronic nipple stimulation, which can lead to persistent discharge. Cirrhosis or other hepatic diseases, which may cause hormonal imbalances leading to discharge. Duct ectasia, a condition where the milk ducts become dilated and inflamed. Early pregnancy, during which hormonal changes can lead to discharge. Fibroadenosis, a benign condition characterized by fibrous and glandular tissue changes. Fibrocystic changes, which are benign alterations in breast tissue that may cause discharge. Galactorrhea, a condition of inappropriate milk production unrelated to breastfeeding. Hypothalamic and pituitary abnormalities, which can disrupt hormonal regulation and lead to discharge. Hypothyroidism, which may cause hormonal imbalances affecting the breast. Intraductal papilloma, a benign tumor within the milk ducts that can cause discharge. Lactation, the normal production of milk postpartum. Lactorrhoea, a term for milk-like discharge outside of lactation. Late pregnancy, during which colostrum or milk production may begin. Medications, particularly those that affect hormonal pathways, can induce discharge. Mondor's disease, a rare condition involving thrombophlebitis of the superficial veins of the breast. Paget's disease of the nipple, a rare form of breast cancer involving the nipple and areola. Prolactinoma, a pituitary tumor that secretes prolactin, leading to discharge. Puberty, during which hormonal changes may cause temporary discharge. Pseudocyesis, a false pregnancy that can mimic lactation. Retroareolar abscess, an infection behind the nipple that can cause discharge. Sarcoidosis, a systemic inflammatory disease that may involve the breast. Systemic lupus erythematosus, an autoimmune condition that can affect multiple organs, including the breast. Tuberculosis, which can rarely involve the breast and cause discharge. Differential Diagnosis for Breast Pain: Breast pain may arise from various causes, including: Breast abscess, which can cause localized pain and swelling. Breast cancer, which may present with pain, particularly in advanced stages. Cyclical mastalgia, pain associated with the menstrual cycle. Cysts, which are fluid-filled sacs that can cause localized pain. Duct ectasia, which can lead to pain due to inflammation of the milk ducts. Extramammary causes of pain, such as referred pain from the chest wall or spine. Fat necrosis, a benign condition resulting from trauma to the breast tissue. Fibroadenoma, a benign breast tumor that may cause discomfort. Fibrocystic changes, which can lead to tenderness and pain. Herpes zoster, a viral infection that can cause pain in the breast area. Intraductal papilloma, which may cause localized pain. Lactation, during which engorgement or mastitis can cause pain. Lipoma, a benign fatty tumor that may cause discomfort. Mastitis, an infection of the breast tissue that causes pain and inflammation. Mondor's disease, which can cause localized pain due to vein inflammation. Non-cyclical mastalgia, pain unrelated to the menstrual cycle. Pregnancy, during which hormonal changes can lead to breast tenderness. Phyllodes tumor, a rare breast tumor that can cause pain. Rib secondaries, metastatic cancer to the ribs that may cause referred pain. Tietze's disease, an inflammatory condition of the costal cartilage causing chest and breast pain. Trauma, which can lead to localized pain and swelling. Unilateral or bilateral gynecomastia, which can cause tenderness in males. Diagnostic Approach: History and Symptoms: A thorough history is essential and should include: Family history of breast or other cancers. Menstrual history to assess hormonal influences. Pregnancy history to evaluate for pregnancy-related changes. Physical Examination: Assess the pattern and duration of pain or discharge. Perform a complete breast examination, ideally 7-9 days after menstrual flow to minimize hormonal influences. Laboratory Investigations: Complete blood count (CBC) to assess for infection or anemia. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) to evaluate for inflammation. Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) to assess hormonal status. Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) to rule out thyroid dysfunction. Liver function tests (LFTs) to evaluate for hepatic causes. Prolactin levels to assess for hyperprolactinemia. Calcium levels to rule out metabolic abnormalities. Beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG) to confirm or exclude pregnancy. Imaging Studies: Chest X-rays may be performed to rule out metastatic disease in the lungs or ribs and to detect pleural effusion in cases of cancer. Ultrasound can help differentiate between cystic and solid masses. Diagnostic mammograms are recommended for patients over 30 years of age, with comparison to previous mammograms if available. Additional Diagnostic Procedures: Breast biopsy for histological evaluation of suspicious lesions. Galactogram or ductogram to assess the milk ducts. Fine needle aspiration for cytological examination of discharge or masses. Treatment: Patients with fibrocystic changes should avoid caffeine, as it may reduce pain. Routine follow-up is essential for monitoring. Warm compresses can provide relief for patients with mastitis. Pharmacotherapy: Pain relief medications may be prescribed for fibrocystic changes. For breast cancer, treatment may include radiation, chemotherapy, or hormonal therapy. Antibiotics are indicated for infections such as mastitis or abscesses, targeting organisms like streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus. Surgical and Device-Based Interventions: Aspiration may be performed for cysts or fibrocystic changes. Surgery is often required for breast cancer management. Incision and drainage are indicated for abscesses.
